exploration.title: Caravan Crossroads
exploration.subject: History
exploration.summary: Plan a caravan’s route and supplies, then compare how terrain and seasons change a journey.
exploration.question: Why might travelers choose a longer route instead of the shortest one?
exploration.explanation: Trading routes connected communities and carried ideas and skills as well as goods. The Silk Roads were a changing network of land and sea routes, not a single road or one journey made by every merchant. Travelers had to consider terrain, water, seasons and supplies. This fictional journey borrows those general trade-offs. Its routes, prices, cargo losses and travel times are invented for comparison, not a reconstruction of a particular culture, place or century.

experiments.title: Choose a seasonal route
experiments.instruction: Pack 14 supply days and keep the cargo fixed. Predict how changing from dry to wet season affects the river route, then compare travel time and cargo delivered.
experiments.observe: Use the journey results to explain why the fastest route can depend on conditions, not just distance. Identify which numbers are model assumptions rather than historical evidence.

experiments.title: Pack for the journey
experiments.instruction: Choose a route and predict the supplies needed for its travel time. Add supply days until the shortage is zero, then increase the cargo load.
experiments.observe: Compare total load with carrying capacity. Explain the trade-off between carrying more goods and leaving room for the supplies needed to complete the journey.

exploration.misconception: Trade was not simply one-way travel between two distant empires. Networks involved many communities, local exchanges and changing routes.
